title: Chapter 13 — Wheelbarrow
paragraphs: Next morning, Monday, after selling the embalmed head to a barber for a wig block, I settled our bill — using Queequeg's money, however. The grinning landlord and boarders seemed enormously amused by the sudden friendship between me and Queequeg — especially since Peter Coffin's wild stories had previously made me so terrified of the very person I now kept company with.

We borrowed a wheelbarrow, loaded our things — my poor carpet-bag, Queequeg's canvas sack and hammock — and headed down to the Moss, the little Nantucket packet schooner moored at the wharf. People stared as we walked — not so much at Queequeg, since they were used to seeing cannibals in their streets, but at seeing us on such friendly terms. We ignored them, taking turns wheeling the barrow, Queequeg occasionally stopping to adjust the sheath on his harpoon barbs. I asked why he carried such a cumbersome thing ashore when surely all whaling ships provided their own harpoons. He answered that while what I said was true, he had a special fondness for his own harpoon — it was made of proven steel, tested in many mortal combats and deeply intimate with the hearts of whales. In short, like many inland farmers who bring their own scythes to other men's fields, Queequeg preferred his own harpoon for his own private reasons.

Switching the barrow from my hand to his, he told me a funny story about the first wheelbarrow he'd ever seen. It was in Sag Harbor. His ship's owners had lent him one to carry his heavy sea chest to his boarding house. Not wanting to appear ignorant — though he was entirely ignorant of how to use the thing — Queequeg placed his chest on the barrow, lashed it tight, then hoisted the whole contraption onto his shoulders and marched up the wharf. 'Queequeg,' I said, 'you should have known better! Didn't people laugh?'

At that, he told me another story. On his island of Rokovoko, at wedding feasts, they press the fragrant water of young coconuts into a large stained calabash like a punchbowl. This punchbowl is always the great centerpiece of the braided mat where the feast is held. Once, a grand merchant ship visited, and its captain — by all accounts a very stately, punctilious gentleman — was invited to the wedding feast of Queequeg's sister, a pretty young princess who had just turned ten. When the wedding guests gathered at the bride's bamboo cottage, the captain marched in and was given the seat of honor, directly across from the punchbowl, between the High Priest and King Queequeg's father. Grace was said — for those people say grace as well as we do, though Queequeg told me that unlike us, who look down at our plates, they look upward to the great Giver of all feasts, copying the ducks. Then the High Priest opened the banquet with the island's ancient ceremony: dipping his consecrated fingers into the bowl before the blessed drink could circulate. The captain, seated next to the Priest and watching this ritual, concluded that as captain of a ship he clearly outranked a mere island king — especially in the king's own house — and calmly proceeded to wash his hands in the punchbowl, apparently mistaking it for a large finger bowl. 'Now,' said Queequeg, 'what you think? Didn't our people laugh?'

At last, passage paid and luggage safe, we stood aboard the schooner. Hoisting sail, she glided down the Acushnet River. On one side, New Bedford rose in terraces of streets, its ice-covered trees glittering in the clear, cold air. Huge hills and mountains of barrels were piled on the wharves, and side by side the world-wandering whale ships lay silent, safely moored at last — while from others came sounds of carpenters and coopers, fires and forges melting pitch, all signaling that new voyages were being prepared. One long, perilous voyage ends, and a second begins; the second ends, and a third starts — forever and ever. Such is the endlessness of all earthly effort.

Reaching the open water, the bracing breeze freshened. The little Moss tossed quick foam from her bows, like a young colt snorting. How I breathed in that brisk, wild air! How I scorned the common highway, all dented with the marks of slavish heels, and turned to admire the magnificence of the sea, which permits no records.

Queequeg seemed to drink and reel at the same spray fountain with me. His dark nostrils flared wide; he bared his filed and pointed teeth. On we flew, and once we'd gained the open sea, the Moss paid homage to the blast — ducking and diving her bow like a slave before a sultan. Leaning sideways, we darted sideways; every rope hummed like a wire; the two tall masts bent like Indian canes in a tornado. So absorbed were we in this thrilling scene, standing by the plunging bowsprit, that for a while we didn't notice the jeering looks from the other passengers — a landlubber bunch who marveled that two people should be so friendly, as though a white man were somehow more dignified than a whitewashed Black man. Among them were some real bumpkins who, by their extreme greenness, must have come from the very heart of the countryside. Queequeg caught one of these yokels mimicking him behind his back. I thought the fool's hour had come. Dropping his harpoon, Queequeg grabbed the man in his arms and, with almost miraculous dexterity and strength, launched him bodily into the air. With a light tap to his backside at the peak of the somersault, the fellow landed on his feet, lungs bursting, while Queequeg calmly turned away, lit his tomahawk pipe, and passed it to me for a puff.
'Captain! Captain!' yelled the bumpkin, running toward the officer. 'Captain! Here's the devil!'
'Hey, you!' cried the captain, a gaunt scarecrow of the sea, stalking up to Queequeg. 'What the hell do you mean by that? Don't you know you could have killed that man?'
'What him say?' said Queequeg, mildly turning to me.
'He says,' I said, 'that you nearly killed that man there' — pointing to the still-shivering greenhorn.
'Kill him?' cried Queequeg, twisting his tattooed face into an unearthly look of disdain. 'Him very small fish. Queequeg no kill such small fish. Queequeg kill big whale!'
'Listen here,' roared the captain. 'I'll kill you, you cannibal, if you try any more tricks on this ship. Watch yourself!'

But just then the captain had to watch himself. The enormous strain on the mainsail had snapped the weather sheet, and the huge boom was now swinging wildly from side to side, sweeping the entire stern deck. The poor fellow Queequeg had tossed was knocked overboard. Everyone panicked. Trying to grab the boom seemed suicidal — it flew left and right, almost in one tick of a watch, threatening to splinter at any moment. Nothing could be done. Everyone rushed to the bow, staring at the boom as if it were the lower jaw of an enraged whale. In the midst of this chaos, Queequeg dropped to his knees, crawled under the boom's path, grabbed a rope, secured one end to the railing, and then, flinging the other like a lasso, caught it around the boom as it swept over his head. At the next jerk, the spar was trapped. The schooner was turned into the wind. While the crew prepared the rescue boat, Queequeg stripped to the waist and dove from the side in a long, living arc. For three minutes or more we watched him swimming like a dog, his powerful arms cutting straight through the freezing foam, his brawny shoulders breaking through the water. I looked at that grand, glorious man but saw no one to be saved — the greenhorn had gone under. Queequeg shot himself vertically out of the water, took a quick look around, and dived down and vanished. A few minutes later he surfaced, one arm still stroking, the other dragging a lifeless form. The boat picked them up. The bumpkin was revived. Everyone voted Queequeg a hero. The captain begged his pardon. From that hour I clung to Queequeg like a barnacle — until poor Queequeg took his last long dive.

Was there ever such lack of self-importance? He didn't seem to think he deserved a medal. He only asked for water — fresh water — and something to wipe off the brine. That done, he put on dry clothes, lit his pipe, leaned against the railing, and gazing mildly at those around him, seemed to be thinking: 'It's a mutual, joint-stock world in every latitude. We cannibals must help these Christians.'
